claim: Updating only a pretrained N-gram memory table changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% relative RMS, against 64%/35% for merged LoRA and 97%/39% for shared LoRA.
stance_target: The claim that writing into a frozen-adjacent N-gram table disturbs the base model least, the premise behind the repo's frozen-Engram design
scope_conditions: 48-layer MoE with a 51.2B-parameter native N-gram memory; seven-task SIGMORPHON chain; identical data and budget across arms; big-K drift at the LM-head input, last prompt token
quoted_support: Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA.

claim: N-gram memory drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays flat at 21-26% on math for all seven, while shared LoRA grows almost monotonically from 45% to 97%.
stance_target: The claim that a frozen backbone plus memory-table writes is stable over a long update horizon, unlike adapter training
scope_conditions: Seven-task chain, drift measured at every task boundary
quoted_support: This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating.

claim: An input whose addressed rows were never rewritten is exactly unchanged at every layer and in every logit, because the addresses are fixed by raw token IDs and everything upstream of the read is frozen.
stance_target: The mechanism that makes frozen-table writes non-destructive to the base model
scope_conditions: Hashed N-gram table read at layer 2; addresses depend only on raw token IDs with history reset after EOS
quoted_support: For N-gram memory, an input whose addressed rows were never rewritten is exactly unchanged. This is why generic drift stays small, and why interference concentrates on inputs that share rows.

claim: The native N-gram memory is 51.2B parameters: 320,001,536 rows of width 160 read at layer 2, with each token reading 16 rows (8 bigram + 8 trigram heads) totalling 2,560 values.
stance_target: The repo's assumption that a ~6B frozen Engram table is representative of the frozen-table literature's scale
quoted_support: It carries a native, jointly pretrained N-gram memory of 51.2B parameters: a table of 320,001,536 rows of width 160, read at the second layer. Each token reads one row from each of 8 bigram and 8 trigram hash heads (16 rows, 2,560 values).

claim: A 51.2B-parameter BF16 table is ~102 GB, so the table alone exceeds a 64 GB CMP 170HX card by ~1.6x before the 48-layer MoE backbone is loaded.
stance_target: Whether the frozen-table literature's configurations can be reproduced on a single 64 GB card
scope_conditions: Arithmetic: 51.2e9 params x 2 B/param in BF16
quoted_support: It carries a native, jointly pretrained N-gram memory of 51.2B parameters ... The model runs in BF16.

claim: The N-gram arm's trainable set is only 51,018-149,809 rows per task (8-24M scalars); all seven tasks together touch 666,747 rows, 0.21% of the table, and each task shares 1,277-4,911 rows with earlier tasks.
stance_target: The repo's claim that frozen-table designs keep the trainable budget tiny
scope_conditions: N-gram arm, seven SIGMORPHON tasks, 5,000 examples each
quoted_support: Each task has between 51,018 (AMH) and 149,809 (AFB) rows, i.e. 8-24M scalars. All seven tasks together touch 666,747 rows (0.21% of the table), and each task shares between 1,277 and 4,911 rows with earlier tasks.

claim: Because untouched rows have identically zero gradient and optimizer state, Adam on the touched rows is exactly equivalent to full-table Adam — so optimizer state scales with touched rows, not table size.
stance_target: The repo's 16 B/trainable-param vs 2 B/frozen-param memory arithmetic, which assumes frozen rows carry no Adam state
scope_conditions: N-gram arm; hashing, gate, read-out projections, router, all Transformer weights and the head frozen
quoted_support: On the touched rows, Adam is exactly equivalent to full-table Adam, because untouched rows have identically zero gradient and optimizer state.

claim: The cost of the frozen-backbone design appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA.
stance_target: The implication that frozen-table writes are strictly better than adapters; they trade acquisition and interference for base stability
scope_conditions: Seven-task chain; old-task NLL measured after each task boundary
quoted_support: The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA.

claim: Forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho = 0.85; rho = 0.71 on Llama-3-8B).
stance_target: Which drift metric actually predicts interference in a frozen-table design
scope_conditions: Small-ki drift versus big-K drift; replication on Llama-3-8B
quoted_support: We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho = 0.85; rho = 0.71 on Llama-3-8B)

claim: The paper's design principle is to write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed, leaving the remaining problem — interference between stored tasks — inside the memory.
stance_target: The repo's Memory Grafting framing that frozen tables are the right place to put capacity
scope_conditions: Conclusion drawn from the three-channel comparison
quoted_support: These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.

claim: Training used Megatron-SWIFT on 4xH200 with TP2/PP2/EP2 — tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism simultaneously — none of which the CMP 170HX's no-P2P Gen2 x4 fabric supports.
stance_target: Whether the frozen-table literature's training recipe is reproducible on this box without re-deriving it under pure DDP
scope_conditions: Infrastructure section; checkpoints hash-verified before use as the parent of the next task
quoted_support: Training uses Megatron-SWIFT on 4xH200 with TP2/PP2/EP2.

claim: All three arms used identical data order and budget: 125 optimizer steps x global batch 40 = 5,000 presentations per task, max length 128, Adam beta (0.9, 0.95), peak lr 1e-4 cosine to zero, gradient clipping 1, optimizer and scheduler reset at every task boundary.
stance_target: The experimental budget needed to reproduce the drift comparison
scope_conditions: Seven SIGMORPHON tasks, 5,000 training examples each, chat template with thinking disabled
quoted_support: All arms use identical data order and budget: 125 optimizer steps x global batch 40 = 5,000 presentations per task, max length 128, Adam (beta = (0.9, 0.95), eps = 1e-8), peak learning rate 1e-4 with cosine decay to zero, no warm-up, no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.
